items.followUp: What are dietary fibres, and how do they help maintain a healthy digestive system?

rubric.why: Identifies dietary fibre as roughage that humans cannot digest.
rubric.description: Defines dietary fibre as the indigestible part of food (roughage).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that fibre is not digested by humans or is called roughage.

rubric.why: Shows its plant origin or names a major component.
rubric.description: Names plant foods as a source or gives a fibre component such as cellulose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct source or component.

rubric.why: Explains how fibre supports movement through the digestive tract.
rubric.description: States that fibre adds bulk to stool/faeces and helps bowel movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the bulk or bowel-movement role.

rubric.why: Gives a key digestive benefit of dietary fibre.
rubric.description: Links fibre with peristalsis or prevention of constipation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct effect on bowel function.

modelAnswer: Dietary fibres, also called roughage, are the indigestible parts of plant foods.
They include cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin and are found in fruits, vegetables and whole grains.
Fibre adds bulk to the faeces and helps move food through the digestive tract by promoting peristalsis.
It helps prevent constipation and supports regular bowel movements.

items.followUp: Define transpiration and state two ways in which it is important to plants.

rubric.why: Checks the definition and the plant part involved.
rubric.description: Defines transpiration as loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water-vapour loss from aerial plant parts.

rubric.why: Identifies the main route of water-vapour loss.
rubric.description: States that transpiration occurs mainly through stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming stomata as the main route.

rubric.why: Recognizes the cooling effect of transpiration.
rubric.description: Explains that transpiration cools the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating its cooling role.

rubric.why: Recognizes the role of transpiration in upward water movement.
rubric.description: States that transpiration creates a pull that helps move water upward through the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking transpiration with water ascent or transpiration pull.

rubric.why: Recognizes the contribution of transpiration to mineral transport.
rubric.description: States that transpiration helps transport or distribute mineral salts through the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly linking transpiration with mineral-salt movement.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
It creates a transpiration pull that helps in the upward movement of water.
It helps transport and distribute mineral salts through the plant.
It supports the continuous movement of water from roots to leaves.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a food chain and a food web.

rubric.why: Captures the relatively limited number of species in a simple community.
rubric.description: States that a simple community has relatively few species or organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining feature of limited species diversity.

rubric.why: Captures the greater diversity and complexity of a complex community.
rubric.description: States that a complex community has many species or organisms, with more complex interactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying its greater diversity or interaction complexity.

modelAnswer: A simple community has relatively few species and relatively simple interactions among its organisms.
A complex community has many species and more varied, intricate interactions among its organisms.

items.followUp: What is multicellular organization? Give two examples of multicellular organisms.

rubric.why: Checks that unicellular organization involves just one cell.
rubric.description: Defines unicellular organization as an organism consisting of a single cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the organism is made up of one cell.

rubric.why: Checks for examples of unicellular organisms.
rubric.description: Gives two suitable examples, such as Amoeba and Paramecium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correct examples.

modelAnswer: Unicellular organization is a level of organization in which an organism consists of a single cell that performs all life activities.

items.followUp: What is induction in the biological method?

rubric.why: Checks the direction and nature of deductive reasoning.
rubric.description: Defines deduction as reasoning from a general principle to a particular conclusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying reasoning or drawing a conclusion, and 1 mark for stating the general-to-particular direction.

modelAnswer: Deduction is a process of reasoning in which a particular conclusion is drawn from a general principle or statement.

items.followUp: What causes itching and swelling at the site of an insect bite?

rubric.why: Identifies the saliva introduced by the mosquito as the trigger.
rubric.description: States that mosquito saliva enters the skin during the bite and triggers a reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning mosquito saliva or its injected substance.

rubric.why: Explains the body's response that produces the welt.
rubric.description: Links the body's histamine or allergic response with swelling/welt formation and itching.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting the immune response with the local swelling or welt.

modelAnswer: When a mosquito bites, it injects saliva into the skin.
The body reacts to the saliva by releasing histamine, which causes a raised welt, swelling and itching.

items.followUp: State two observations that led A. F. A. King to connect mosquitoes with malaria.

rubric.why: Checks the observed association between mosquitoes and malaria.
rubric.description: States that malaria was common in places where mosquitoes were abundant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting the association of malaria with mosquito-infested places.

rubric.why: Checks an observation comparing mosquito exposure with malaria occurrence.
rubric.description: States that people protected from mosquito bites were less likely to get malaria, or that exposed people were more likely to get it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid observation about protection from or exposure to mosquitoes.

modelAnswer: A. F. A. King observed that malaria was common in places where mosquitoes were abundant.
He also observed that people protected from mosquito bites, for example by mosquito nets, were less likely to get malaria.

rubric.why: Checks that a micrograph is a recorded image of an object viewed microscopically.
rubric.description: Defines a micrograph as a photograph or image of an object seen through a microscope.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as a photograph/image and 1 mark for linking it to viewing through a microscope.

modelAnswer: A micrograph is a photograph or image of an object as seen through a microscope.
